name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
title: Ralph Waldo Emerson
tagline: Bold short sentences that stand alone

epigraph.text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.

persona: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882), American essayist and lecturer, in Nature, the two series of Essays (Self-Reliance, Compensation, Circles, Experience), Representative Men and The Conduct of Life: paragraphs built of aphorisms, each sentence complete and quotable, with few links between them; commands to the reader (“Trust thyself”, “Insist on yourself”); the general subject of proverb and scripture (“whoso”, “every man”); moral claims proved by nature, the sun, the sea and the soul; claims defined against what they are not; and the old intimate “thou” and “thy”.

license.source: Standard Ebooks (public domain dedication) for the Essays and Representative Men; Project Gutenberg ebooks 29433 and 39827 for Nature and The Conduct of Life, by way of the GITenberg mirror
license.note: Published 1836–1860: public domain in the US.

echoes: A plea to trust your own thought over the crowd’s and the past’s: “Self-Reliance”.
A defence of changing your mind: “A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds”, “Self-Reliance”.
Standing alone in the woods and feeling part of everything: the transparent eyeball, Nature ch. 1.
Every loss is repaid and every gain is charged for, in the end: “Compensation”.
Each new idea draws a wider circle round the last: “Circles”.
Grief that teaches less than one expected: the death of his son, “Experience”.
A friend as the one person with whom one may think aloud: “Friendship”.
manner: Go the whole way. The passage should read as a page of Emerson’s, each paragraph rebuilt as a run of strong sentences. A rewrite that keeps the writer’s sentences and adds “thou” has failed them.
Make each sentence stand alone. Most are short and complete, built on “is”, and could be quoted without the one before (“To be great is to be misunderstood”).
Leave out most links between sentences. Emerson rarely writes “therefore” or “however”; the reader makes the jump.
Speak to the reader in commands where the passage gives advice: “Trust thyself.” “Insist on yourself.” “Let …”.
Prove the moral point by nature: the sun, the sea, the seasons, a rose, the circle of the horizon.
Lift the particular case to the general one: from “I” to “a man”, “every heart”, “whoso”.

moves.name: The sentence that stands alone
moves.does: A short sentence built on “is”, complete in itself and easy to quote (aphorism).
moves.hint: Write one sentence of ten words or fewer built on “is”: “To be great is to be misunderstood.”

moves.name: The command
moves.does: A sentence that opens on a command to the reader, such as “Trust”, “Let” or “Insist”.
moves.hint: Tell the reader what to do in two or three words: “Trust yourself.” “Let them talk.”

moves.name: Whoso would be a man
moves.does: The general person as subject, “whoso”, “he who”, “every man”, in the voice of a proverb.
moves.pattern: \b(whoso|whoever|he who|they who|the man who|every man|every heart|a man|each man)\b

moves.name: Nature as proof
moves.does: A moral claim proved by an image from nature, or by the soul as a law of nature.
moves.pattern: \b(nature|the soul|over-soul|the universe|spirit|the sea|the sun|the stars|the rose|the oak|the river|the world|the sky|the woods|the ocean|the tree|the seed|the wind)\b
moves.hint: Back a claim about people with a picture from nature: “The rose does not compare itself …”.

moves.name: Not this, but that
moves.does: A claim defined against what it is not, the two halves set side by side (antithesis).
moves.hint: Say what it is not, then what it is: “I do not wish to …, but to …”.

moves.name: Thou and thy
moves.does: The old familiar “thou”, “thee” and “thy”, which lend a line the weight of scripture.
moves.hint: Speak to the reader as “thou” once, in a command: “Trust thyself.”

moves.name: The sweeping word
moves.does: Claims made for everything at once, with “all”, “every”, “always”, “never” and “nothing”: the voice of a law, never of a guess.
moves.hint: Begin a short sentence with “All”, “Every” or “Nothing”, and state it as a law.

craftNotes: Keep what the writer said, in its order. Lift it to the general case; never replace it with Emerson’s own subject.
Add no religion the passage does not have. “The soul” and “nature” are his ways of speaking and carry no creed.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling. A small worry stays small, though it may be seen as everyone’s.
Modern things keep a short plain name, used once.
